metric_rationale: Measures the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Tallying heuristic (choosing the option that wins on more features). The experimental design perfectly dissociates Tallying from WADD on all trials, so Tallying will produce values near 1, while WADD will produce values near 0.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the WADD predictions on the specific trials where WADD and Tallying strictly disagree. On Trials 1, 2, and 4, Tallying predicts one option based on the number of feature wins (3 vs 1), while WADD predicts the opposite option due to the large cardinal magnitude differences on high-validity features. The metric will be close to 1.0 for subjects using WADD and close to 0.0 for subjects using Tallying.

This metric isolates trials where the Tallying heuristic and the WADD heuristic make opposite predictions. Specifically, it identifies trials where one option is vastly superior on the single most valid feature (which dominates WADD), while the other option has a slight edge on all three remaining features (which dominates Tallying). The metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying prediction on these conflict trials. The pure WADD model will almost never choose the Tallying option (except due to random lapse), resulting in a value close to 0. The advocated mixture model, which includes a Tallying component, will choose the Tallying option significantly more often, leading to a much higher expected value.

The advocated theory (pure WADD) uses a deterministic argmax policy over its computed probabilities. Because the parameters (validities, beta, epsilon) are fixed per subject, the choice probabilities for a given trial type are identical across all repetitions. Furthermore, the epsilon lapse rate only scales and shifts the probabilities without changing their relative ordering, meaning the argmax is unaffected. Thus, the advocated theory predicts zero intra-subject variance across repetitions of the exact same trial. In contrast, the competing theory uses a probabilistic sampling policy (`np.random.choice`), which inherently produces choice variability across repetitions. By measuring the mean intra-subject, intra-trial variance of responses, we perfectly capture this structural difference.

Contrasts Trial 5 and Trial 3. Under true validities, pure WADD has a stronger preference for A on Trial 3 (15 vs 14, diff=1.0) than on Trial 5 (17.5 vs 17, diff=0.5). Thus, pure WADD naturally predicts P(A|T3) > P(A|T5). However, the Tallying heuristic strongly favors B on Trial 3 (3 wins to 2) and favors A on Trial 5 (3 wins to 2). The advocated Mixture model, which incorporates Tallying, will therefore show a suppressed probability of choosing A on Trial 3 and an enhanced probability of choosing A on Trial 5, reversing the inequality to P(A|T5) > P(A|T3). This structural reversal is difficult for a pure WADD model to fit simultaneously with the rest of the trials.

This metric calculates the overall rate at which a subject's choices align with the Tallying heuristic, restricted to trials where Tallying has a strict preference (i.e., one option wins on more features than the other). The Pure WADD model will only align with Tallying when the subjective weighted sum happens to agree, which is frequent but not guaranteed. The Mixture model, however, explicitly incorporates Tallying as a standalone strategy on a subset of trials (governed by the alpha parameter). Therefore, the Mixture model predicts a systematically higher and more consistent alignment with the Tallying heuristic across these trials compared to Pure WADD.

The experimental design varies the magnitude of the rating differences while keeping the ordinal signs (wins/losses) constant across trials. The Competing Theory (TTB + Weighted Tallying) only considers the signs of the differences, predicting identical choice probabilities across all magnitude variations. The Advocated Theory (Tallying + WADD) integrates cardinal magnitudes, predicting a large shift in choice probabilities as the magnitude of differences scales up. This metric computes the difference in the proportion of choosing Option B (response = 1) between low-magnitude difference trials (sum of absolute differences == 4) and high-magnitude difference trials (sum >= 13). The Competing Theory predicts a difference of 0, while the Advocated Theory predicts a large positive difference.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the highest-validity cue (cue 0) specifically on trials where it conflicts with the unweighted majority of cues (tallying). In the designed experiment, these are the 'double-must' dissociation trials (trials 1-8). The advocated theory (Mixture of TTB and Weighted Tallying) strongly prefers the option winning on the highest-validity cues, ignoring the massive magnitudes on the losing cues, so it will score near 1.0. The competing theory (Mixture of Tallying and WADD) is driven by the majority of cues (Tallying) and the massive magnitudes (WADD), so it strongly prefers the opposite option, scoring near 0.0. This ensures a massive and highly stable quantitative gap between the two theories.
